sections.h2: Selling a house in Swatara Township
sections.html:
Swatara Township is a Dauphin County township just south of Susquehanna Township in the Harrisburg area. A sale there means dealing with a township codes office, a private real estate tax collector and the county recorder. The municipal building is at 599 Eisenhower Boulevard in Harrisburg.

The township runs along the Susquehanna River and takes its name from Swatara Creek, so water is part of the conversation for houses near either one.

The population is 27,936, and owners live in 69.9 percent of homes. The middle owned home is valued at $214,400, rent runs $1,252 and household income is $80,444. The township has 10,640 households of 2.47 people on average.

Roughly 88.3 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier. Long-time owners may never have sold before, so the sections below name each office you will meet on the way to the closing table.

sections.h2: How the codes office affects a sale
sections.html:
Building and zoning permits come from the township's codes department. Approved Code Services, Inc. does the plan reviews and construction inspections as the township's sole third-party agency, and property maintenance complaints under the International Property Maintenance Code run through the same department.

New construction, additions and alterations call for a building permit. Routine maintenance, repairs and like-for-like equipment replacement generally need none. Stormwater management permits and quarterly waste fee exemption requests also go through the department.

If an inspector flags unpermitted work, phone the department at 717-564-2551 before you reply. The office is open weekdays from 8 until 4:30. Yard waste is easy to clear before showings, and the township runs a fall brush collection each year.

sections.h2: Real estate tax collector and transfer tax
sections.html:
Real estate tax is collected at a separate office, 6400A Chambers Hill Road in Harrisburg, and the municipal building does not accept those payments. The collector takes payment for the current year only. Tax certification requests go to that office at 717-832-4908.

Keystone Collections Group, with a Dauphin County office on Vartan Way, collects local services tax and earned income tax instead. Knowing the split helps when a title agent asks which office issues which certificate.

The county recorder describes the 2 percent as divided among the state, the municipality and the school district. Deeds are recorded at the Dauphin County Courthouse, 101 Market Street, Harrisburg, where the deed index starts in 1785.

Central Dauphin School District covers the township, and Swatara Middle School plus Lawnton, Rutherford and Chambers Hill elementary schools are among its buildings. Confirm which school your address feeds before naming one in a listing, since attendance can vary by street.

A house near the creek or the river can raise questions that an interior lot does not. If your property sits close to the water, ask your agent or a surveyor to confirm its flood zone status, and be ready with any repair history, including invoices for pumps, drainage work or waterproofing. Buyers and their insurers tend to ask, and a folder of records answers the question before it becomes a negotiating point.

A clean closing depends on a short list of documents, and most of them come from offices named on this page.

  • A tax certification from the township's tax collector, so the title agent sees what has been paid this year.
  • A payoff letter from your lender, and a copy of the deed from the county Recorder of Deeds.
  • Permit paperwork for additions, decks and alterations, available through the Building and Codes Department.
  • Sewer and stormwater bills, which the township lists on a separate online payment page from real estate tax.
  • Receipts for work done since you bought, because buyers who finance will have an appraiser and an inspector look at condition.

Order the tax certification early. It comes from a different office than the municipal building, and the title agent cannot finish the search without it.

sections.h2: If you owe tax or have unpermitted work
sections.html:
Two problems come up often with older township houses. The first is a tax balance. That collector handles the current year only. Ask what is due now and hand the figure to the title agent. Anything still unpaid is settled out of your sale money.

The second is a project done without a permit, perhaps a finished basement or a new deck. Phone the codes department before a buyer's inspector spots it. Staff can say whether a permit was required and what it takes to close the matter. If the cleanup is too much, tell buyers openly, because someone purchasing as is can price it into the offer.

sections.h2: From signed contract to the closing table
sections.html:
Every route follows one sequence. The agreement of sale comes first, then a title search of the record, then any lender or inspector review, then settlement. On that day the closing agent retires your mortgage, clears tax balances and sends the deed to Harrisburg for recording.

Without a lender in the chain, a cash closing can be set around your moving date. Whoever buys should give you a written date, the title company's name, and an explanation of what happens if the date slips.

Houses that come with a tenant or an estate attach a few extra tasks. If someone rents the property, give the buyer a copy of the lease early and agree on whether the tenant stays or leaves before closing. If the house came to you by inheritance, confirm who has the legal power to sign the deed, and gather any tax and sewer bills that arrived in the previous owner's name.

An as-is buyer is often the simpler answer for these properties, since there is no need to empty or repair the house before the sale can move ahead.

sections.h2: Which routes work for a quick sale?
sections.html:
Three paths are open: an agent's listing, a private sale, or a direct sale to an investor or cash buyer. Listing may bring the highest price, but you give up control of the calendar to showings, repair requests and a lender.

  • Listing: suits a sound house and a seller with time for financing and inspections.
  • Private sale: avoids a commission and leaves pricing and paperwork with you.
  • Direct purchase: no financing, no showings and a closing day you choose, with the price adjusted for repairs.

On any route, line up a tax certification, a lender payoff letter and your deed copy. Get every buyer to write down who covers the 2 percent transfer tax. Without it the deed cannot be recorded.

faqs.q: Where does Swatara real estate tax get paid?
faqs.a: At the township's real estate tax collector at 6400A Chambers Hill Road, Harrisburg, or online through the link on the township's tax page. The municipal building does not accept real estate tax payments.

faqs.q: What does the transfer tax cost on a Swatara sale?
faqs.a: Two percent overall. The recorder breaks it into 1 percent for the state and one half percent apiece for the township and the school district.

faqs.q: Are permits needed for repairs before a Swatara sale?
faqs.a: New construction, additions and alterations generally need a building permit, while routine maintenance and replacement of existing equipment generally do not. Call the Building and Codes Department at 717-564-2551 if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Who collects Swatara's earned income tax?
faqs.a: Keystone Collections Group, which keeps a Dauphin County office on Vartan Way in Harrisburg. This is separate from the real estate tax collector.

faqs.q: What school district serves Swatara Township?
faqs.a: Central Dauphin School District. Its schools include Swatara Middle School and elementary schools in Lawnton, Rutherford and Chambers Hill.
